framework: Safety Management Systems and Just Culture
problem_it_solves: How to apportion responsibility when a person departs from written procedure, given that procedures routinely conflict or cannot all be met at once.
protocol: The substitution test: ask whether another similarly trained and experienced person, in the same circumstances and with the same information, would plausibly have acted the same way. If yes, the finding is systemic and the procedure or its design is the defect. Individual culpability is reserved for wilful violation, recklessness, or repeated departure after correction.
what_it_confirms: An independent profession, working from accident data rather than from law, reached the same structure: where the system compelled the choice, the defect belongs to the system and not to the person who made it. The necessity-silence conflict is not an idiosyncratic construct.
what_it_adds: An operational test. The simulator asserted that discretion was 'functionally required' without supplying a way to prove it. The substitution test does exactly that, and it is a test a record can actually satisfy.
where_it_breaks: Just Culture is purchased with a protected reporting channel and an explicit decision not to pursue individual liability. Adjudication has no such channel and cannot make that trade: the individual's loss is the whole subject of the proceeding, so the systemic finding must still resolve into a remedy for one person.

problem_it_solves: How to read the routine gap between documented procedure and actual practice.
protocol: Treat the gap as normal and load-bearing rather than as deviance. Procedures are written for imagined conditions; operators adjust continuously to real ones, and that adjustment is what makes the system work at all. Investigate what made the adjustment necessary before asking whether it was permitted.
what_it_confirms: Departure from written process is the normal operating condition of a real institution, not a rare failure. The simulator's loose regime is right to treat settled practice as the operative rule.
what_it_adds: A sharper framing of the claimant's burden. The question is not whether the institution departed from its written process — it always does — but whether it knew, tolerated and relied on the departure, and then invoked the written text against one person after the fact. That is a narrower and much more winnable claim.
where_it_breaks: Safety science is deliberately non-adjudicative. It refuses to assign liability because assigning it suppresses the reporting the method depends on. Borrowing its diagnosis without its remedy is legitimate; borrowing its posture is not.

problem_it_solves: How a departure that was once exceptional becomes the unremarked standard.
protocol: Track the sequence by which each tolerated departure resets the baseline, so that the next departure is measured against the new baseline rather than the original rule. The rule on paper stops being the operative standard long before anyone decides to abandon it.
what_it_confirms: A practice can displace a published rule without any act of amendment, which is the premise of the estoppel theory.
what_it_adds: A temporal dimension the simulator lacks entirely. It models practice as a binary — settled or not — with no account of how many tolerated instances over what period establish it. A real claim needs that sequence, and it is exactly what discovery should target.
where_it_breaks: Vaughan's account is descriptive and retrospective, reconstructed with the outcome known. A tribunal sees the same sequence without the disaster at the end, and the pattern is far less legible from inside it.

problem_it_solves: Whether to govern by bright-line rules or by stated objectives with professional judgment.
protocol: Neither pole is stable. Bright lines are evaded by structuring transactions to fall just outside them, so density produces gaming rather than compliance. Pure principles produce inconsistency between comparable entities. The working answer is an objective plus a duty to disclose the judgment made in applying it.
what_it_confirms: The rigid-to-loose axis is a genuine and much-studied dimension, not an invented one.
what_it_adds: A correction. The simulator scores a rigid regime as favourable to the claimant, on the theory that a dense rulebook gives more to breach. Fifty years of accounting practice says the opposite is at least as likely: density hands the respondent a compliance shield, because conduct engineered to satisfy every written rule while defeating its purpose is formally unimpeachable. The rigid regime needs the respondent's structuring defence modelled, and the claimant's answer to it.
where_it_breaks: Accounting standards bind an entity's reporting to strangers who rely on comparability. An institution's internal process binds it to one identified person. The reliance interest is differently shaped, so the disclosure remedy does not transfer cleanly.

framework: Performance-based codes and the Authority Having Jurisdiction
instruments: International Building Code, alternative means and methods
problem_it_solves: How to grant a local official the discretion the work genuinely requires without making that discretion unreviewable.
protocol: The code states the performance objective. Where a proponent seeks to meet it by other means, the authority may approve, but must find and record equivalency against the stated objective, and the record of that finding is what an appeal reviews. Discretion is wide, exercised constantly, and reviewable — because the objective and the written finding exist.
what_it_confirms: This is the simulator's proposed remedy already implemented and in daily use across an entire industry. The claim that standardless discretion is fixable by supplying an objective plus a recorded finding is not theoretical.
what_it_adds: A drafting template with a track record. The amendment to seek is not 'exercise discretion reasonably' — that adds nothing — but the pair the codes actually use: a stated objective, and a duty to record the equivalency finding at the time. The second half is what makes the first reviewable.
where_it_breaks: Building officials decide against physical criteria that can be tested independently. Academic and disciplinary judgments have no comparable external referent, so the equivalency finding is harder to falsify and easier to write to a conclusion.

problem_it_solves: How to authorise judgment in situations no rulebook can anticipate, while keeping that judgment accountable.
protocol: The order states purpose, key tasks and desired end state, and deliberately does not prescribe method. A subordinate's decision is then assessed against the stated intent, not against a procedure nobody could have written in advance. Wide discretion and real accountability coexist because the intent is explicit.
what_it_confirms: The cleanest external validation in this set. A profession whose entire business is irreducible uncertainty concluded that the answer to unavoidable discretion is not more rules but a stated intent to be judged against. That is precisely the remedy vector the simulator generates.
what_it_adds: The argument that the fix is cheap and does not cost the institution its flexibility. An institution resisting a standard on the grounds that it needs room to judge is asking for the wrong thing: intent constrains without prescribing, and it is what makes wide judgment defensible rather than arbitrary.
where_it_breaks: Mission command runs on a shared professional formation, an unambiguous hierarchy, and an agreed objective. An institution in dispute with an individual has none of those, and the intent it states is drafted by the party that will later be judged against it.

framework: Standard of care, peer review and morbidity-and-mortality review
problem_it_solves: How to review expert judgment without a written rule and without the reviewer possessing the expertise.
protocol: The standard is what a responsible body of practitioners would have done, established by expert evidence and, since Bolitho, subject to the court's check that the practice offered is logically defensible. Deference is granted, but only against a demonstrated professional standard.
what_it_confirms: Deference to expert judgment is a legitimate and widely adopted posture, not an evasion. The simulator is right to model it as a serious defeater.
what_it_adds: The most useful asymmetry in this set. Medicine makes deference conditional: the respondent must produce the professional standard and show conformity to it, and a court may still reject a standard that will not bear logical scrutiny. Educational deference under the Ewing line demands no equivalent showing — the institution's characterisation of its own decision as academic largely secures the deference. The simulator should model that gap, because it is an argument: the party seeking deference should have to earn it the way every other profession does.
where_it_breaks: Medicine has an identifiable body of practitioners and a literature against which a standard can be stated. Many institutional decisions are sui generis, with no comparable body to poll.

framework: The intelligible principle and the guidance-versus-rule distinction
problem_it_solves: How much direction an enabling instrument must supply to the body it empowers.
protocol: A delegation is valid where the instrument supplies an intelligible principle to guide the delegate. Separately, a body may not achieve by unpublished guidance what it would need notice and comment to achieve by rule.
what_it_confirms: The doctrinal home of the claim exists and is correctly identified. The vocabulary the simulator reaches for is the vocabulary the field uses.
what_it_adds: A caution the simulator does not currently express. Nondelegation challenges almost never succeed against a public body; courts have accepted very thin principles as intelligible. Pleaded as a constitutional attack this is close to hopeless. Its real force is elsewhere: as the reason a legislature should act, and against a private or quasi-private institution, where the doctrine's deference to legislative judgment does not apply and the guidance-versus-rule line does more work.
where_it_breaks: The doctrine constrains legislatures delegating to agencies. An institution's internal policy set is not a delegation in that sense, so the argument travels by analogy and can be met with the objection that it is the wrong frame entirely.

problem_it_solves: How to preserve on-the-spot judgment while still correcting the decisions that matter.
protocol: Review is confined to a named category of decision and applies an explicit threshold: the original call stands unless the error is clear and obvious. The threshold is deferential and it is written down, so both what is reviewable and how hard it is to overturn are known in advance.
what_it_confirms: A deferential standard is still a real standard when the threshold is stated. The simulator's practice of naming a standard for every condition is sound.
what_it_adds: The observation that the deference itself should be published. Where an institution reviews internally against an unstated threshold, nobody can tell whether a decision was upheld because it was right or because the threshold was unreachable. Requiring the threshold to be written is a smaller ask than requiring a standard for the underlying decision, and it is a useful fallback.
where_it_breaks: Officiating reviews a discrete, recorded, observable event. Institutional decisions unfold over months and the record is assembled by one of the parties.
